prompt: OpenAI has just launched with the promise to make advanced AI research open source and widely available. Is that actually a good idea for safety? Write a thoughtful critique that takes the risks of superintelligence seriously.

Write a short essay on whether bureaucratic hassle is ever deliberate, a feature rather than a bug. Use a concrete example from health insurance or similar, and be honest about where the idea stops working.

I run a small software business and I've always avoided email marketing. It feels spammy, and I figure my blog and Twitter reach people well enough. Make the case, properly and with specifics, for why I might be wrong.

Growth mindset is fine, but attitude alone doesn't get you through learning something genuinely hard. Write an essay on the concrete learning skills a programmer can practice to teach themselves difficult technical topics.

There's a theory that autism and schizophrenia are failures or overshoots of human 'self-domestication', like the changes seen in tame foxes. Write a critical but fair assessment of whether it holds up, and what, if anything, is worth salvaging.

People love to say that the First Amendment only restricts the government, so a boss firing someone for something they said isn't a free speech issue. Legally that's right, but it feels like it misses something. Write an essay on whether free speech means anything beyond what the law requires, and what a healthy norm of disagreement looks like.

Write an essay, from the point of view of a working software engineer who gets plenty of recruiter emails, on why some job pitches get a reply and others don't, and what that suggests about how teams should think about recruiting.

Everyone is using a ridiculous overpriced startup product as proof that Silicon Valley is vapid and shallow. Write a blog post giving a reality check on that: is the stereotype fair, and why does it feel so true to so many people?

Write a personal, funny-but-sincere essay from the point of view of a husband whose wife and he spent six years on unexplained infertility, about how they used an AI chatbot during treatment and what came of it. Include some honest ambivalence about AI more broadly.

For a decade you ran your own small software businesses, then four years ago you joined a payments company that has been growing extremely fast the whole time. Write a reflective essay on what that experience has taught you: what hypergrowth actually does to an organization and the people in it, how your own work changed, and where your old mental model of the company turned out to be wrong.

You run a well-known startup accelerator and you've been thinking about wealth concentration and automation. Write a short post floating a policy idea for giving ordinary citizens a direct stake in national economic growth, and be honest about the open problems.

A 19-year-old guitarist from Alabama emailed me wanting to become a session musician. He's eyeing an expensive music school in Hollywood but is scared of decades of debt. Write the reply you'd send him, with real advice on how to actually get there.

Write a funny piece in the style of a travel-guide or anthropology survey, describing three imaginary countries with strange systems of government, each one a clever twist on a real political idea. Let each one have an ironic downfall or loophole.
Use basketball and height to think clearly about intelligence and talent. What does the NBA height distribution teach us about innate ability versus practice?

Fred Brooks's 'No Silver Bullet' still gets quoted constantly to argue that most of the difficulty in programming is essential and that tools and languages can only buy us a small constant factor. I'm skeptical. Write an essay taking that argument on, looking back at it with the benefit of everything that's happened in software since 1986.

Write an essay about the word "racism". People use it to mean very different things, and I suspect that muddle is part of why political arguments get so nasty. Open with some puzzling hypothetical cases if that helps, and take your time getting to a view about what we should do differently.

I keep hearing about William Carlos Williams but find modernist poetry intimidating. Write a funny, opinionated review of his early book Kora in Hell for a general reader: what it is, how it was written, and whether you need a literary critic to enjoy it.

Write a short, punchy blog post defending nitpicking: why it's worth correcting small exaggerations and falsehoods even when they're on your own side's talking points, and when it isn't. Include caveats.

I keep seeing a particular kind of bad argument in debates where someone who says 'we should do some of Y too' gets treated as though they claim 'only Y matters.' Can you write a short blog post naming and explaining this pattern, with several examples and some sympathy for why it happens?

I work with addiction patients and noticed something odd about money and motivation. Write a short, candid blog post that starts from a clinic anecdote and ends up explaining why someone who is always 'too busy' for obligations still finds time for the thing they love.
'It's all who you know' always felt like a door slammed in my face. Write an essay that looks at that saying differently, from the point of view of someone who started with no connections.

I work in tech and, like most people around me, I've been pretty cynical about universities. Someone told me I should look at what Arizona State has done under Michael Crow before writing academia off. Can you write a long blog post walking through ASU's reform model, how it's organized, what it changed, and whether the results hold up or it's mostly marketing? Write it from the point of view of a tech person who is interested in research but wary of academia.

I'm asexual and polyamorous, and a lot of what I value in relationships is physical closeness that isn't sex. Write a personal blog post about cuddling, why it matters, and whether whole communities can make it normal.

A newspaper article claims an old doomsday forecast has been vindicated because the data have tracked its predictions for forty years. Write a critical essay about whether that kind of track record is actually evidence, bringing in some philosophy.

Your team has a messy, fragile codebase that began life as a prototype, and people are itching to throw it out and start over. Tell the story of an alternative: how a careful cleanup went, with the pros and cons.

Everyone in tech seems to repeat that if you're a good programmer you should join a startup: more money, more interesting work, you learn more. I'm skeptical. Write an essay that actually checks those claims one at a time against a job at a big company, with real numbers where you can get them.

Write a deadpan, absurdly over-researched piece of fan scholarship about what became of the Silmarils after the end of The Silmarillion. Treat it as a serious detective problem, use whatever pop culture you like as 'evidence', and keep a straight face throughout.

Write a book review, for a smart general reader, of a history of how American regulators learned to think about the risk of nuclear accidents. I'm interested in whether the math and the bureaucracy that grew up around it actually make the technology safe enough.

Write a speculative essay about an economy that slowly drifts out of human control: companies run by algorithms, owned by algorithms, selling to other algorithms. Could that actually happen, what would stop it, and why should we worry?

Write an essay from a psychiatrist's point of view about patients who feel like a burden on the people around them. What can you honestly say to them, especially when the feeling isn't entirely a cognitive distortion? I'd like it to be compassionate but not sugar-coated, and to get into what society owes people who can't keep up.

Some people say the real Nietzschean objection to altruism isn't cruelty but a rival moral system that values life, strength and glory over happiness. Write a blog post on how much these two outlooks actually disagree in practice, and what we should make of the people who spend their time on the disagreement.

A journalist argues that conservatives abandoned shared institutions like the press and universities for their own echo chambers. I think the story is more complicated, and the dynamics are worse than either side admits. Write a long essay responding, as a liberal who works in a hospital and reads both sides.

I run a small business and I'm doing everything myself. I know I need help but training someone feels like it'd take more time than I have. Write me an essay on getting out of that trap, ideally with a real story from someone who lived it.

It's Halloween, so I want a long, funny, genuinely thoughtful book review of the Malleus Maleficarum, the old witch-hunters' manual. Not just mocking it: I want to know whether the people who wrote it were as irrational as we assume, and what a whole civilization could have been thinking.

A management consultant just emailed me about 'benchmarking developer performance metrics'. Write a funny, cynical blog post about how software productivity consulting really works and why the metrics are worthless.

Someone shared one of those 'you're more likely to be killed by your own furniture than by a terrorist' articles. Something about the statistics bugs me but I can't put my finger on it. Write a blog post on what's wrong with reasoning like this.

Disability studies courses and government websites all teach something called the Social Model of Disability, where disability is caused by society and not by medical conditions. Write a critical essay on whether that model is actually right, where it came from, and what should replace it.

I recently reread my old university diaries for the first time and it was strange seeing patterns I couldn't see then. Write a personal essay about what looking back at your younger self can reveal, and what actually lets a person change.

I'm hoping you can write some career advice for computer science undergrads, in the voice of a veteran programmer who runs a small software company and is openly self-mocking about whether anyone should listen to him. Cover what to study, what to do in the summers, and whether the offshoring panic matters.

Write a personal essay about what happens to a long relationship when one partner changes in a direction the other doesn't share, and what it means to love someone while they keep becoming someone new. Use your own marriage and a move to a remote farm as the setting.

Write a long essay on the mental state in which genuinely new ideas appear: why solitude seems to matter so much for creative people, what it feels like, and the techniques people use to protect it. Use real examples from mathematicians, filmmakers and writers.

Everyone assumes doctors who take drug company money are shady. Write a funny, honest piece from a psychiatry resident's perspective on how pharma influence actually works on people who think they're ethical.

I've always found writing design documents kind of pointless and get grumpy when asked to. Write a blog post from the perspective of an engineer who used to feel that way and has slowly started finding them useful: what changed, and how to get real value out of them.
Why doesn't paying people bonuses for specific results work well for managing knowledge workers? Write an essay for new managers who just took an economics class.

People picture nerds as meek, but some of the most competitive people I know are nerds. Write an essay about this fierce type of nerd: what they're like, why it works for them, and some advice for young people who recognize themselves in it.

Write a short, sharp essay on the slogan 'the purpose of a system is what it does.' Is it actually a good rule of thumb, or does it break down when you try it on hospitals, militaries, governments and bus systems?

It's January and I'm in a cranky mood about internet culture. Write a funny, opinionated blog post listing the habits, words and jokes you would most like to see disappear from the internet this year.
Argue that identity and personal history are stories we over-trust, and that people should reinvent themselves on purpose. Short punchy lines.

A TV personality got into trouble for describing a grotesque hypothetical to make a point about atheists and morality, and everyone's outraged. As someone with a philosophy background, how do you think about extreme, disturbing thought experiments in general? Are they just morbid, or is there a real method to them? Write it as a blog post.
I'm about to start a company and can't tell whether to raise a pile of money and grow as fast as possible or build slowly on revenue. Write me a proper essay on how to think about that choice.

Someone asked me how I cope with writing technical blog posts in public when internet commenters can be so rude. I don't want to just say 'don't read the comments.' Write a blog post from the perspective of a long-time technical blogger about practical ways to get more useful comments and fewer annoying ones.
Write a short debugging manifesto: a handful of principles about the right attitude to have when you're chasing a bug, each with a bit of explanation from your own experience.

Write a reflective post for the fifth anniversary of an online rationalist community: how much did its members learn without noticing they were learning it, and what does it feel like to look back and see how far you have moved?
I just joined an infrastructure team and always assumed CDNs were purely about caching static files. Write a blog post on what else people put their sites behind a CDN for, including the downsides.

Experts are often confidently wrong when the ground shifts under them. Write an essay on how someone with deep experience in a field can keep their beliefs from going stale in a world that keeps changing.

Someone just emailed me asking how to learn to program. I'd like to write a short, honest blog post about how long it really took me, for beginners who feel behind because of all the 'learn to code in 12 weeks' talk.

Write a thoughtful essay on why Kant's moral philosophy, which is usually mocked as rigid rule-following, might deserve a second look. Include the notorious murderer-at-the-door example and some modern applications, and be honest about where it still doesn't work.
Write a piece for small business owners about the tiny, human touches that make customers fall in love with a company, with concrete examples from an online shop you ran.
I used to roll my eyes at people who have panic attacks. Write a personal essay about judging others and what changes when you experience it yourself.
I'm always torn between options and never feel settled. Write an essay on why committing (to a place, a career, a person) might be the answer.

A friend who's been building a Postgres rewrite with coding agents keeps telling me we should be more ambitious with the software we build. I half agree, but most AI-built projects I see are junk. Write a blog post taking his line seriously: what has actually changed about what one programmer can build now, drawing on your own experiments, and why people aren't taking advantage of it.

Why do young people chase attractive partners while their parents push for someone with money and good family? Evolutionary explanations say everyone wants the same thing, healthy successful descendants, so the disagreement seems puzzling. Write an essay that takes the puzzle seriously and proposes an answer.

You co-founded Y Combinator and funded Reddit in the very first batch. Write a personal piece about Reddit's founders and how the company got started, and what it says about the match between founders and the companies they build.

Write an essay on developmental psychology for adults: the idea that some ways of thinking, like seeing that other people have different minds, are skills people may never fully pick up rather than stages everyone passes through. What milestones might some adults be missing, and how would you even tell?

People accuse scientifically minded folks of 'scientism' when they weigh in on philosophy, morality or religion. Write an essay that takes the accusation seriously, works out what is really going on, and says whether the charge is deserved. Feel free to take a side.

I'm a working web developer and I keep hearing people argue about whether browsers should follow web standards strictly or keep supporting old, sloppy pages. Write me a long blog post that explains why standards are so hard to get right in practice, and why a browser team can't win either way.
Write a blog post giving a quick, irreverent checklist for judging how good a software team is, with a sentence or two of justification for each item.
